edits.quote: Two players alternate taking 1 or 2 counters. Never take more than remain. Taking the last counter wins.
edits.fix: Move the rules out of P1 into brief unnumbered shared rules at the top of page 1, worded for reading aloud to K-1: 'Take turns. On your turn take 1 or 2 counters. Whoever takes the last counter wins.' Delete 'Never take more than remain' (ungrammatical, and the counters enforce it).

edits.quote: Play from 4 counters twice, swapping who starts. Draw or write the number taken at each turn. Circle the last move. / Play from 5 counters twice, swapping who starts. Record the moves and circle the last move.
edits.fix: Two separate problems of about two minutes each that only say play and record, with no question. Merge into one problem with a goal: 'Play from 4 and from 5, twice each, swapping who starts. Who won each game? From which pile can the first player always win?'

edits.quote: Use the same 1-or-2 rule.
edits.fix: Delete once the rules are stated once at the top.

edits.quote: Two players alternate taking 1 or 2 counters. Never take more than remain. Taking the last counter wins.
edits.fix: Delete. This repeats the activity-wide rules.

edits.quote: Start with 3 counters. Let the other player start. Try each of their first moves below. Record how many you take next. [table: Starting pile 3, 3 / Other player takes 1, 2 / I take next / Counters left]
edits.fix: The table lists the opponent's moves for the child. The answers are forced, 'Counters left' is always 0 and 'Starting pile' just repeats 3. Drop those two columns and ask the question instead: 'Would you rather start from 3 or let the other player start? Try every move they could make.'

edits.quote: Make two groups of 3. ... choose your reply so that exactly 3 counters remain. Then finish each game.
edits.fix: This prints the trap strategy that the children are supposed to discover, and 'Counters left' is then always 3. Rewrite: 'Start with 6 counters and let the other player start. Can you win no matter what they take? Test both of their first moves.' Leave space to record each whole game.

edits.quote: Draw the two groups before the game: [empty box]
edits.fix: Delete. Drawing two groups of 3 is busywork, and the box comes after the table even though it says 'before the game'.

edits.quote: Two players alternate taking 1 or 2 counters. Never take more than remain. Taking the last counter wins.
edits.fix: Delete. This is the third copy of the rules.

edits.quote: Play twice from each pile and check your choice.
edits.fix: 'Check your choice' is vague, and there is nowhere to record the games. Write: 'Test your choice by playing an adult twice from each pile. Change it if you lose.'

edits.quote: Build 12 counters as four groups of 3. Let the other player start. After each of their moves, take enough to remove 3 counters between your two turns. Record the numbers left after each of your turns.
edits.fix: P5 asks children to find the strategy, then P6 states it as a procedure. 'Between your two turns' is also unclear when read aloud, since it does not say whose turns. Replace with an open challenge: 'From 12 counters, would you go first or second? Play an adult who tries to beat you. Which piles do you try to leave?'

edits.quote: Draw my four groups: [empty box]
edits.fix: Delete. Drawing 12 counters in groups is busywork.

edits.quote: Worksheet ends after P6 with about a fifth of page 3 blank.
edits.fix: A quick child runs out after about 20 minutes, so roughly 15-20 minutes are missing, and nothing is hard for a first grader. Add a substantial concrete problem, for example: 'New rule: take 1, 2, or 3. Find every pile from 1 to 12 that you want to hand the other player.' That gives traps at 4, 8, 12 to compare with the 1-or-2 game. Another option is to extend P5 to all piles up to 15.

k-1.summary: The band works on the right idea from the outline: small 1-or-2 games and trap piles at multiples of 3, with counters and tables. But P4 and P6 tell children the 'leave 3 / remove 3 each round' strategy instead of letting them find it, P3 is a forced two-row exercise, and the rules are printed three times. A quick child is done in about 20 minutes and never meets a hard question, so the K-1 pages end too early and are too watered down.

edits.quote: Never take more than remain.
edits.fix: Delete. It is ungrammatical, and the counters enforce it.

edits.quote: a partner may write while you play.
edits.fix: Delete. This is logistics for the adult.

edits.quote: Winner: first or sec- ond (column header hyphenated across two lines)
edits.fix: Widen the column or shorten the header to 'Winner (1st or 2nd)'.

edits.quote: Play from 5, 6, and 7. Swap who starts and replay each pile. Record the moves in order
edits.fix: No goal is given. The 'Winner' column records the results of casual play, and those say nothing about who can force a win. Add the question: 'From which of these piles can the first player always win? Is there one where you would rather go second?'

edits.quote: Build a pile of 2, then a pile of 4. From each pile, try every allowed first move. Reset the pile before the next attempt. Record how many counters each move leaves.
edits.fix: A one-minute directed step (pile 2 has only one move) that P3's 'All legal next piles' column repeats. Delete P2.

edits.quote: Put L at 0 because there is no move. Work from small piles upward. List all legal next piles. Mark W if at least one is L; mark L if all are W.
edits.fix: This prints the backward-induction rule, which is the central idea. Keep the W/L definitions and 'Pile 0 is L', delete the method sentences, and let children work out with counters how each label follows from smaller piles.

edits.quote: A position is W if the player about to move has a winning strategy; it is L if every move lets the other player force a win.
edits.fix: 'Position', 'winning strategy' and 'force a win' are abstract for grades 2-3. Use concrete wording: 'Mark a pile L if whoever has to move from it will lose against a careful player. Otherwise mark it W.'

edits.quote: Chart rows for piles 0-7 only.
edits.fix: P5, P6 and P7 need labels for 8-14 ('First decide the missing labels for 8 and 9'), but there is nowhere to record them. Extend the chart to 0-16 so children can also see L return at 7, 9, 14, 16.

edits.quote: Build a nonempty pile you marked L, such as 2 or 7.
edits.fix: 'Such as 2 or 7' gives away P3's answers directly under P3's chart. Pile 2 also has only one first move. Replace with 'Build a pile bigger than 5 that you marked L.'

edits.quote: Use moves 1, 3, and 4. ... Reset each time.
edits.fix: Delete the repeated rule and the directed step.

edits.quote: From 8 counters, try taking 1, 3, and 4. Reset each time. Use your chart to record what each move leaves ... / Do the same from 10. [two pre-filled Take 1/3/4 tables]
edits.fix: Two two-minute steps that repeat P3's 'One move to L' column for one pile each, with the moves pre-printed. Merge them into the extended chart and ask one question: 'Find every winning first move from each pile 8 to 14. Which piles have none?'

edits.quote: not just the first one you find
edits.fix: Delete. 'Record all winning moves from 10' already says it.

edits.quote: Choose a starting pile from 8 through 14. Make a strategy card: record each possible first move and the pile it leaves. Circle moves that hand your opponent an L. Test the card in a game.
edits.fix: The card covers only the first move, so it is not a strategy (the outline says a strategy must answer every reply). Children have labels only up to 9 or 10, so piles 11-14 cannot be done. A child who picks 14 (an L pile) gets a card with nothing circled, and the problem never says to go second. Rewrite: 'Choose a pile from 8 to 14 and decide whether to go first or second. Make a card that says what you take after every move your opponent might make, then play an adult who tries to break it.'

edits.quote: Band ends at P7 with little beyond labels to 10.
edits.fix: A quick child runs out at about 28 minutes, so about 12-15 minutes are missing. Add a substantial problem. One option: 'Ana says: always take as many as you can. Find piles where she loses, and beat her.' This tests a claimed strategy against every reply. Another: predict which piles up to 30 are L from the chart and test one with counters.

grades-2-3.summary: The band gets to the outline's kernel for this band: classifying piles 0-7 under {1, 3, 4} and testing a reply chart. But it prints the W/L procedure and gives the answers away ('such as 2 or 7'). Its later problems (P2, P5, P6) are small directed steps, and the chart has no room for the labels 8-14 they depend on. The final 'strategy card' is not a strategy, and there is about 12-15 minutes too little work for a quick child.

edits.quote: Never take more than remain.
edits.fix: Delete. It is ungrammatical, and the counters enforce it.

edits.quote: Swap who starts for a second attempt at a pile that surprised you.
edits.fix: 'A pile that surprised you' is vague, and the table has only one spare row. Write: 'Play each pile twice, swapping who starts. Which pile would you rather go second on?' Add rows for all six games.

edits.quote: Winner: first or sec- ond (column header hyphenated across two lines)
edits.fix: Widen the column or shorten the header.

edits.quote: Build small piles and work upward: mark W if a legal move reaches L, and L if every legal move reaches W.
edits.fix: This prints the backward-induction rule, which grades 4-5 can derive from the definitions. Keep the definitions and 'Zero is L', and replace the method with 'Label piles 0-7 and explain how you decided each one.'

edits.quote: Table rows for piles 0-7 are about one third of an inch tall
edits.fix: Make the rows taller so children have room to write the next piles.

edits.quote: Continue using moves 1, 3, and 4. Fill the chart in order. [chart starts again at pile 0]
edits.fix: Piles 0-7 get labeled twice, once in P2 and again in P3. Start P3's chart at 8, or drop P2's label column.

edits.quote: Chart: row 1 has separate 'Pile' and 'Label/move' rows; rows 2-4 put the pile number and the label space in one cell
edits.fix: Redraw all four rows the same way, with the pile number above a separate writing cell.

edits.quote: Compare the rows after filling at least two of them. / The repeating pattern I see: [box placed under P4]
edits.fix: 'Compare the rows' asks no question, and the pattern task appears only as a box label under the next problem. Put the task in P3: 'Which piles are L? Predict the labels of 50 and 100 without filling more cells.' Move the box under P3.

edits.quote: Compare these four piles. Record every legal next pile and its label. Circle the starting piles that have no move to L. [rows 14, 16, 15, 17]
edits.fix: This repeats information already in the P3 chart, and listing 14 and 16 first gives away which piles are L. Delete it, or fold it into P5 as a check.

edits.quote: Arrange 14, 16, 15, and 17 counters in whole groups of 7 with a smaller leftover group. [column 'Whole groups of 7']
edits.fix: This tells children the period is 7 before they state the pattern, and the 'Whole groups of 7' column is always 2. Ask them for the repeat length first, then to group counters by it. Drop the constant column.

edits.quote: Use your chart to choose a winning move for each leftover count marked W. Record the leftover count after the move. For counts marked L, list every leftover count an allowed move can reach; use piles 7 and 9 so that all three moves are possible. [column 'Move to L, or all moves from L']
edits.fix: Two different tasks share one table and a mixed column, and the problem never says what the table is for: showing that the pattern must continue. Rewrite around one question: 'Explain why every pile with leftover 0 or 2 is L, no matter how big it is.' Give separate space for the W rows and the L rows.

edits.quote: Choose a first move using your table, then play.
edits.fix: 'Your table' could mean the P3 chart or the P6 table. Write 'using your leftover rule'.

edits.quote: Build smaller piles to check a proposed strategy. Record which piles you want to hand the other player.
edits.fix: It does not say whose 'proposed strategy'. Write: 'Find which piles you want to hand the other player, and explain why the rule works for every pile.'

edits.quote: Change the allowed moves to 1, 3, and 5. ... My games and the piles I want to leave: [1-inch box]
edits.fix: This is the only rule change, it is the quick parity case, and it has only a small box. Add a 0-12 label chart for {1, 3, 5} and a second contrasting rule such as {1, 4} or {1, 2}, so children compare how the pattern changes.

edits.quote: P8 placed between the {1, 3, 4} problems; P9 begins 'Return to moves 1, 3, and 4.'
edits.fix: Move P8 after P10 and delete 'Return to moves 1, 3, and 4.'

edits.quote: To find the next label, inspect the first, second, and fourth cells: mark the next W if any is L, and L if all three are W.
edits.fix: This gives away the key insight, which is that the next label depends only on the last four. Ask instead: 'Which cells of a window decide the next label, and why?'

edits.quote: Find another matching pair of four-label windows in your chart. Copy both windows, extend them by two labels, and compare the results.
edits.fix: It never asks for the conclusion. Ask: 'Explain why the labels after two matching windows must match forever. Why must some pair of windows match for any set of moves?'

grades-4-5.summary: This is the deepest band. It goes from play to a 0-27 chart, the period-7 pattern, a leftover-mod-7 explanation and the four-label window argument from the outline. The mathematics is correct throughout. But almost every step is printed as a procedure: the W/L rule, 'groups of 7', and which window cells to inspect. P2 and P4 duplicate the chart, P6 and P10 never ask for the conclusion they lead to, and the rule-change comparison is one thin problem placed in the middle.

overall.strongest: Grades 4-5 covers the most of the outline, with correct mathematics, taking children from play through a full chart to the period-7 pattern and the window argument for why it repeats.
overall.weakest: K-1 ends after about 20 minutes for a quick child and states the 'leave a multiple of 3' strategy in P4 and P6 instead of letting children find the traps.
